analysis.one_liner: Delays the ban on banks trading for their own profit until regulators finish the final rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to the Senate Banking Committee in March 2012 and never received a hearing or a vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2010 financial reform law (Dodd-Frank) included the Volcker Rule, which stops banks that enjoy federal deposit insurance and emergency lending from trading for their own profit. Under the law, banks had to conform by the earlier of two dates: one year after regulators issued final rules, or two years after the law passed (July 21, 2012). This bill flips that word from "earlier" to "later," meaning banks would have until as late as possible—whichever deadline comes last—before the trading ban took effect. The bill died in committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Large banks with proprietary trading desks—units that trade stocks, bonds, and derivatives with the bank's own money rather than on behalf of customers—would gain the most, because a delay lets those desks keep operating and generating revenue for as long as possible. Hedge funds and private equity funds would also benefit, since the rule restricts banks from investing in and sponsoring them, and a delay preserves those bank relationships and capital flows.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends Section 13 of the Bank Holding Company Act, changing the compliance deadline for the Volcker Rule prohibitions from the "earlier of" two dates to the "later of" them—the later of either 12 months after final implementing rules are issued, or 2 years after July 21, 2010 [S2] [S3].

Because final rules were not issued during this Congress, the change would have pushed the mandatory compliance date past the July 21, 2012 date set in the underlying law, giving banks the maximum permitted runway before the trading ban became enforceable [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary investors, depositors, and taxpayers bear the cost: for every additional month of delay, banks backed by federally insured deposits and access to emergency Federal Reserve lending can continue speculative trading, and the public remains exposed to losses of the kind that produced the 2008 bailouts. Consumers also wait longer for the market-stability protections the rule was designed to provide.

drawbacks.text: Delaying the rule extends the period during which government-backstopped banks can trade with their own capital, leaving taxpayers exposed to the very risk the 2010 law was written to close [S2].

The underlying law already gave regulators built-in flexibility, so even supporters had to acknowledge the bill added little except a longer wait; the strongest good-faith argument for it was that banks needed time to untangle complex trading operations and comply with rules that had not yet been finalized [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs almost entirely to a handful of large trading banks, which gain extra months (potentially years) of proprietary trading revenue. The cost falls diffusely on the public in the form of prolonged exposure to bank speculation. Given that the existing law already allowed regulators to adjust timing as rules were finalized, the bill's main practical effect was to maximize the delay for the industry it would serve.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on March 22, 2012, read twice, and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Senator Mike Crapo introduced the bill on March 22, 2012, joined by five cosponsors—three Democrats (Warner, Hagan, Carper) and two Republicans (Toomey, Corker) [S1] [S3] [S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs; the action history shows no further action of any kind [S5] [S1].

The bill's single provision was a two-word edit to the Bank Holding Company Act—striking "earlier of" and inserting "later of"—which moved the Volcker Rule compliance deadline from whichever date came first to whichever came last [S3] [S2].

The Volcker Rule's final implementing rules were not issued until after this Congress ended, so had the bill passed, the compliance date would have been pushed to 12 months beyond that later rulemaking rather than the mid-2012 date in the underlying law [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the Volcker Rule's trading ban stayed on the books as written, and the extra delay for big banks' trading desks never happened. The public retained the protection on the original timetable; the banks that would have gained from the postponement came out behind relative to what the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary investors; the trading ban stayed on schedule.

industries.industry: Large banks with proprietary trading desks
industries.note: The bill would have let bank trading units that profit from speculative trades keep operating up to two years longer than the underlying law required, while the banks retain deposit insurance and emergency Federal Reserve access. That extra trading window is revenue for the banks and residual risk carried by depositors and taxpayers.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and private equity funds
industries.note: The Volcker Rule restricts banking entities from investing in and sponsoring hedge and private equity funds; a delay preserves those bank capital relationships during the extension period.
A changing deadline keeps compliance teams in limbo about when they must unwind prohibited trading operations, adding planning uncertainty even as it delays the mandate.
